name: clone(2) syscall
description: Creates a new process or thread with selectable resource sharing via the CLONE_* flags. Foundation of every container start: runc invokes clone with CLONE_NEWUSER|CLONE_NEWPID|CLONE_NEWNS|CLONE_NEWIPC|CLONE_NEWUTS|CLONE_NEWNET (and CLONE_NEWCGROUP on cgroup v2) to put the new process in fresh namespaces. clone3() is the modern variant accepting a struct clone_args. Failure path: EPERM when caller lacks CAP_SYS_ADMIN for namespace creation flags; EINVAL when an invalid flag combination is passed (e.g. CLONE_THREAD without CLONE_VM).

name: fork(2) syscall
description: Creates a new process by duplicating the calling process via copy-on-write. The child gets a copy of the parent's address space, file descriptors, signal dispositions, and most attributes. Returns 0 in child, child PID in parent, -1 on error. Modern Linux implements fork() as a thin wrapper around clone() with no CLONE_* flags. Failure path: EAGAIN when the per-user RLIMIT_NPROC is hit or system fork-bomb-protection trips.

name: execve(2) syscall
description: Replaces the current process image with a new program. Preserves PID, parent PID, file descriptors (unless O_CLOEXEC was set), and most signal masks. RESETS effective UID to file's setuid owner if setuid bit is set, EXCEPT when caller has PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS — the cornerstone of why containers set no_new_privs. Capability sets are recomputed via the cap-transition formula (see capabilities(7)). Failure modes: ENOEXEC (binary format unrecognized), ETXTBSY (binary open for writing), EACCES (no execute permission).

name: unshare(2) syscall
description: Disassociates parts of the calling process's execution context from a previously shared one — creates new namespaces in-place without forking. Takes the same CLONE_NEW* flag set as clone(). Useful for setting up a fresh namespace before exec'ing into a container payload. CLONE_NEWUSER must be the first/only flag in single calls; combine others in a second unshare after entering the user namespace.

name: setns(2) syscall
description: Joins the calling process to an existing namespace identified by a file descriptor opened on /proc/<pid>/ns/<type>. Order matters when joining multiple: user namespace first to acquire credentials, then mount/pid/net/etc. The mechanism behind nsenter(1) and the runtime entrypoint of `docker exec`. Failure: EPERM when caller lacks CAP_SYS_ADMIN in the target user namespace.

name: pivot_root(2) syscall
description: Atomically switches a mount namespace's root filesystem from one mount to another, moving the old root to a designated subdirectory. The clean container-init pattern: mount new rootfs, chdir into it, pivot_root, umount the old root. Safer than chroot because the process can't see/escape to the old root once unmounted. Used by runc; replaces the older chroot+mount-move dance.

name: seccomp(2) syscall
description: Configure secure-computing state on the calling thread. Modes: SECCOMP_MODE_STRICT (only read/write/_exit/sigreturn allowed) and SECCOMP_MODE_FILTER (BPF-program-driven syscall filtering). Once set, can only be tightened (no relaxation), and PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS must be set or caller needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN. Foundation of Docker's default seccomp profile (~330 syscalls allowed) and Kubernetes' RuntimeDefault profile.

name: prctl(2) syscall
description: Multiplexed process-control syscall. Operations selected by first arg: PR_SET_NAME (thread name), PR_SET_PDEATHSIG (signal on parent death), PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS (one-way bit forbidding privilege gain via execve), PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER (zombie reaping), PR_CAPBSET_DROP (capability bounding set drop), PR_CAP_AMBIENT (ambient capability manipulation), and dozens more. Single most-used 'misc process attribute' interface.

name: keyctl(2)/add_key(2)/request_key(2)
description: In-kernel key-management syscalls. add_key creates a key in a keyring; keyctl manipulates keyring permissions, links, revocations; request_key asks the kernel to find or instantiate a key (possibly invoking userspace via /sbin/request-key). Foundation of dm-crypt key passing, NFSv4 idmap, and per-process secret stores.

name: sigaction(2) signal handler installation
description: Establishes a handler for a signal via struct sigaction (sa_handler/sa_sigaction + sa_flags + sa_mask). Replaces the older signal(2) interface, which has portability quirks. Critical flags: SA_RESTART (restart interrupted syscalls), SA_SIGINFO (3-arg handler with siginfo_t), SA_NOCLDWAIT (auto-reap zombies for SIGCHLD). Non-async-signal-safe code in handlers is undefined behavior.

name: sigprocmask(2)/pthread_sigmask(3) signal-mask manipulation
description: Per-thread signal mask manipulation. Blocks/unblocks specified signals during critical sections. Inherited across fork; preserved through execve. SIG_BLOCK/SIG_UNBLOCK/SIG_SETMASK are the operations. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be blocked — definitional unkillable property.

name: capset(2)/capget(2) capability syscalls
description: Set/get the four capability sets of a thread (effective, permitted, inheritable, ambient). The libcap helper functions wrap these. The kernel enforces strict subset rules: P' (permitted) must be a subset of bset∩(P∪I-already-granted); E (effective) is a subset of P. Bounding set is per-thread and never increases.

name: setuid/setgid/setresuid family
description: setuid(2), seteuid(2), setreuid(2), setresuid(2) (and gid equivalents) manipulate the real, effective, saved, and filesystem UIDs of the calling process. Required CAP_SETUID for asymmetric changes. Used by su/sudo/login transitions. Capability set is recomputed on UID 0 ↔ non-zero transitions unless KEEP_CAPS securebit is set.

name: setrlimit(2)/getrlimit(2) resource limits
description: Per-process soft/hard resource limit knobs. Soft is enforced; hard is the ceiling for raising soft (lowering hard is one-way unless caller has CAP_SYS_RESOURCE). RLIMIT_NOFILE (max FDs), RLIMIT_NPROC (max processes per real UID), RLIMIT_AS (max virtual memory), RLIMIT_STACK, RLIMIT_CPU, RLIMIT_CORE, RLIMIT_MEMLOCK, RLIMIT_MSGQUEUE, RLIMIT_NICE, RLIMIT_RTPRIO, RLIMIT_RTTIME, RLIMIT_SIGPENDING. systemd unit `LimitNOFILE=` etc. set these per-service.

name: pthread_create(3) thread creation
description: POSIX thread creation primitive — wrapper around clone(2) with CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|CLONE_SYSVSEM|CLONE_SETTLS|CLONE_PARENT_SETTID|CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID. All threads in a process share the PID (TGID); their per-thread ID is the kernel's PID. SIGSTOP/SIGCONT and most fatal signals affect the whole thread group.

name: pthread_join(3)
description: Wait for a joinable thread to terminate, optionally retrieving its exit value. Calling join on a detached thread is undefined. Forgetting to join a joinable thread leaks resources (thread stack, TLS).

name: pthread_detach(3)
description: Mark a thread as detached so its resources are auto-released on termination. Once detached, no longer joinable. Equivalent to creating with attr.detachstate=PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED.

name: pthread_cancel(3)
description: Request cancellation of another thread. Cancellation is delivered at predefined cancellation points (most blocking syscalls: read, write, sleep, wait). Disabled per-thread via pthread_setcancelstate. Cancellation type (deferred vs asynchronous) governed by pthread_setcanceltype. Asynchronous cancellation is dangerous — handlers can run between any two instructions.

name: Effective capability set (E)
description: The set of capabilities currently active for permission checks. Subset of permitted. A thread can flip caps in/out of E without privilege so long as they're in P. The set the kernel checks against on each privileged operation.

name: Permitted capability set (P)
description: The 'master' set: capabilities the thread is allowed to make effective. Bounded above by the bounding set. Permanently lost after `capset(P, …)` removes a cap unless ambient or file-cap bestowal restores it.

name: Inheritable capability set (I)
description: Set of capabilities preserved across execve. For non-root execs, only caps in (I ∩ file-inheritable) survive into the new program's permitted set. UID-0 execs can promote everything in P. Original mechanism for capability transition; mostly superseded by the ambient set in modern setups.

name: Capability bounding set
description: Per-thread upper bound on the inheritable and permitted sets. Drops are one-way (PR_CAPBSET_DROP); never grows. Container runtimes use this to permanently strip CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_MODULE, CAP_SYS_TIME, etc. from container init. systemd's `CapabilityBoundingSet=` directive is exactly this.

name: Ambient capability set
description: Per-thread set of capabilities that are preserved across non-setuid execve into permitted+effective. The post-2016 mechanism for 'I want this non-root program to have CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE permanently.' Capabilities raised via PR_CAP_AMBIENT_RAISE; cleared on UID change. systemd's `AmbientCapabilities=` directive.

name: Effective UID (EUID)
description: The UID the kernel uses for permission checks (file access, signal sending, IPC). Initially equals real UID; setuid binaries set it to file owner. Returned by geteuid(2). Container processes inside a userns have a UID inside the container that maps to a different host UID per /proc/<pid>/uid_map.

name: Real UID (RUID)
description: The UID identifying the user who started the process. Used by the kernel for accounting (RLIMIT_NPROC) and for SIGCHLD attribution. Returned by getuid(2). Stays stable across setuid transitions; only setuid(2) with CAP_SETUID can change.

name: Saved set-user-ID (SUID)
description: Records the EUID at the time of a setuid execve so the program can later swap back to it via setuid/seteuid. Enables the 'temporarily drop privileges' pattern in setuid programs without permanent loss.

name: Filesystem UID (FSUID)
description: Per-thread UID used only for filesystem permission checks. Linux-specific; allows NFS server processes to act as another user for FS operations without becoming that user for signal-receiving purposes. Equals EUID by default; setfsuid(2) decouples them.

name: Signal disposition
description: Per-process attribute mapping each signal to one of: default action (SIG_DFL — Term, Core, Ign, Stop, Cont as defined per signal), ignore (SIG_IGN), or a user-installed handler. Reset to SIG_DFL on execve unless the disposition was SIG_IGN (preserved). Installed via signal(2) (legacy) or sigaction(2) (modern).

name: Pending signal set
description: Per-thread (and per-process for shared signals) bitmap of signals delivered but not yet handled because they're masked. Standard signals do not queue — multiple deliveries while blocked count as one. Realtime signals (SIGRTMIN..SIGRTMAX) DO queue, up to RLIMIT_SIGPENDING.

name: cgroup v2
description: The unified cgroup hierarchy: a single tree where every controller (cpu, memory, io, pids, hugetlb) operates on the same cgroups. Mounted at /sys/fs/cgroup. Replaces the v1 multi-hierarchy mess (one tree per controller). Controllers enabled per-subtree via cgroup.subtree_control. Required for full container resource accounting on modern systemd. systemd uses 'unified' (v2-only) or 'hybrid' (v2 + v1) modes; pure v1 is the 'legacy' mode.

name: cgroup v1
description: The original multi-hierarchy cgroup model: each controller (cpu, cpuacct, memory, blkio, devices, freezer, hugetlb, net_cls, net_prio, perf_event, pids, cpuset) mounts a separate hierarchy under /sys/fs/cgroup/<controller>/. A process can be in a different cgroup per controller. Deprecated in favor of v2 but still widely deployed; Docker on older kernels and some Kubernetes node pools.

name: cgroup hierarchy
description: A tree of cgroups, each containing a set of processes. Children inherit (and can further constrain) the limits of parents. v2 has exactly one tree; v1 has one per controller. Membership lookup via /proc/<pid>/cgroup.

name: cgroup controller
description: A kernel subsystem that constrains or accounts resources for processes in a cgroup. v2 controllers: cpu, memory, io, pids, hugetlb, rdma, misc, cpuset. Enabled per-subtree by writing the controller name (e.g. '+memory') to cgroup.subtree_control. Cannot be enabled in a cgroup that contains processes (the 'no internal processes' rule for non-root cgroups).

name: cgroup delegation
description: Granting an unprivileged user write access to a cgroup subtree so they can manage their own sub-cgroups. Requires write access to cgroup.procs, cgroup.threads, cgroup.subtree_control, and the cgroup.* control files of children. The mechanism systemd uses to let user units self-manage their resource limits without root.

name: No-internal-processes rule (cgroup v2)
description: In cgroup v2, a non-root cgroup with controllers enabled cannot contain processes directly — only its leaf descendants can. Forces a clean tree shape for resource accounting. Common surprise when migrating from v1 (where processes could live anywhere); systemd-cgls makes the layout visible.

name: Linux namespace isolation model
description: Per-process scoping of kernel resources so different processes see different views. 8 namespace types: mount (filesystem mounts), pid (process IDs), uts (hostname/domainname), ipc (System V IPC + POSIX msg queues), net (interfaces, sockets, routing), user (UID/GID mappings + capabilities), cgroup (cgroup root view), time (CLOCK_MONOTONIC offsets). Container = a process in a fresh set of all 8.

name: PID namespace
description: Isolates the process ID number space. Processes inside see different (usually lower) PIDs than their host PIDs. The first process in a new pid namespace becomes pid 1 — gains init responsibilities (zombie reaping, signal-default behavior: ignored signals don't kill it). PID-1 death = entire namespace dies. Hierarchical: parent namespace can see and signal child-namespace processes (via host PIDs).

name: PID 1 init semantics
description: The first process in a PID namespace has special kernel behavior: ignored signals (no handler installed) are silently dropped instead of being delivered with default action; orphaned children reparent to it; if it exits, every other process in the namespace receives SIGKILL. This is why container init processes that don't reap zombies leak them indefinitely (defunct processes accumulate) and why naive entrypoints don't respond to `docker stop` (SIGTERM is dropped). Solved by tini/dumb-init/--init.

name: PID translation across namespaces
description: A single process has different PIDs in each PID namespace it belongs to (its own and all ancestors). /proc/<host-pid>/status NSpid line lists all of them. Tools like nsenter use the host PID; commands inside the container reference container-namespace PIDs. Source of confusion in 'process X is running' — depends on the PID namespace you're asking from.

name: User namespace
description: Isolates UID/GID number spaces and the capability set within. A process can be UID 0 inside its userns (full caps inside) while being an unprivileged UID outside. Foundation of rootless containers: the dockremap user (or rootless dockerd's owning user) provides the host range that container UIDs map to via /etc/subuid + /etc/subgid + /proc/<pid>/uid_map. Userns nesting is supported (configurable max via user.max_user_namespaces sysctl).

name: User namespace UID mapping
description: Per-userns mapping table from container-internal UIDs to host UIDs. Written once to /proc/<pid>/uid_map (and gid_map). Format: 'inside-uid host-uid count' lines. Writing requires CAP_SETUID in the parent namespace OR (for unprivileged users) restricted to a single 1:1 mapping unless /proc/<pid>/setgroups was first written 'deny'. The /etc/subuid range handed out by newuidmap(1) per user.

name: Mount namespace
description: Per-process view of the mount-point hierarchy. New mounts inside don't affect outside (and vice versa) — modulated by mount propagation flags (shared/private/slave/unbindable). Set up by container runtimes to give each container its own rootfs without polluting the host's /mnt tree.

name: Mount propagation (shared/private/slave/unbindable)
description: Per-mount attribute controlling cross-namespace mount-event visibility. SHARED: events propagate both ways with peers. PRIVATE: no propagation. SLAVE: receives events from master but doesn't send back. UNBINDABLE: cannot be bind-mounted. Container runtimes typically make the container's /sys/fs/cgroup slave so host cgroup-mount changes are visible without container changes leaking back. Source of the 'docker volume mount changes don't appear on host' surprise when propagation is wrong.

name: Network namespace
description: Isolates network devices, addresses, routing tables, ports, sockets, /proc/net/*, /sys/class/net/*. Each netns has its own loopback. veth pairs link two namespaces; one end goes inside, the other lives in the host bridge (docker0). Per-netns iptables/nftables rulesets. The whole network leaf operates within this primitive.

name: UTS namespace
description: Isolates the hostname and NIS domainname (uname() fields). The smallest namespace by surface area — just 2 strings. Why `hostname` inside a container differs from the host without affecting it.

name: IPC namespace
description: Isolates System V IPC objects (shared memory segments, message queues, semaphores) and POSIX message queues. /dev/shm is per-IPC-namespace. ipcs(1) inside a container shows only that namespace's IPC objects. Containers default to a private ipcns; opt out with `--ipc=host` (and lose the isolation).

name: cgroup namespace
description: Virtualizes the cgroup-tree view in /proc/self/cgroup. Inside the namespace, the process sees its cgroup as the root (a chrooted view of the cgroup tree). Hides the host's cgroup hierarchy from container processes — important for rootless and security-sensitive containers.

name: Linux Security Module (LSM)
description: Hook framework in the kernel that lets security modules (SELinux, AppArmor, Smack, TOMOYO, BPF-LSM, Yama, Landlock) impose mandatory access control on top of DAC. LSMs are stackable in modern kernels (5.x+). A syscall must pass DAC then every active LSM check. The reason 'permission denied' isn't always about file mode — could be selinux denial in audit.log.

name: SELinux policy model
description: Type-enforcement-based MAC: every process and resource has a context (user:role:type:level). Policy rules say which type can do what to which other type. Modes: enforcing (deny on violation + audit), permissive (audit only), disabled. `setenforce 0/1` toggles enforcing/permissive at runtime. ausearch on AVC denials surfaces violations. The dominant LSM on RHEL/Fedora-derived distros.

name: AppArmor profile model
description: Pathname-based MAC: profiles enumerate file paths a binary may access and capabilities it may use. Profiles loaded into the kernel via apparmor_parser. Modes: enforce, complain (audit-only), unconfined. Default LSM on Ubuntu/SUSE. Docker ships a default-docker profile applied to every container.

name: seccomp SECCOMP_MODE_STRICT
description: Original seccomp mode: only read(2), write(2), _exit(2), and sigreturn(2) are allowed. Any other syscall sends SIGKILL. Useful for sandboxing fully-trusted compute (CPU-bound code that uses pre-opened FDs). Largely superseded by filter mode for general-purpose sandboxing.

name: seccomp SECCOMP_MODE_FILTER
description: BPF-program-driven syscall filtering. The program inspects syscall number and (limited) arg registers; returns one of SECCOMP_RET_KILL_PROCESS, KILL_THREAD, TRAP, ERRNO, USER_NOTIF, TRACE, LOG, ALLOW. Multiple filters are AND-stacked (lowest action wins). The mode container runtimes use; Docker's default profile is a single filter against ~330 syscalls.

name: seccomp-BPF program
description: A classic-BPF (cBPF, NOT eBPF) program of up to 4096 instructions, attached via prctl(PR_SET_SECCOMP, SECCOMP_MODE_FILTER, ...) or seccomp(SECCOMP_SET_MODE_FILTER, ...). Read-only access to syscall number, arch, instruction pointer, and 6 arg registers via the seccomp_data struct. Cannot dereference user-space pointers (preventing TOCTOU on string args).

name: seccomp user-notification (SECCOMP_RET_USER_NOTIF)
description: Filter return value that suspends the syscalling thread and forwards the request to a userspace supervisor over a notification FD. The supervisor inspects the call, decides allow/deny/emulate, and replies. Foundation of unprivileged Docker rootless's mount(2)/iptables emulation, and tools like systemd-userdbd.

name: Signal async-safety
description: The set of functions that can safely be called from a signal handler — strictly: those whose internal state is reentrant and whose interruption can't corrupt the rest of the program. signal-safety(7) lists ~80 functions (write, _exit, kill, sigaction, fork, …); printf, malloc, and most of glibc are NOT in the set. Violating async-safety = silent corruption + heisenbugs.

name: signal(2) vs sigaction(2)
description: signal(2) is the historical, portability-fraught interface (handler reset to SIG_DFL after first delivery on some systems; Linux uses BSD semantics by default but System V semantics under _XOPEN_SOURCE). sigaction(2) is the canonical: explicit sa_flags, deterministic across UNIX. Always use sigaction for new code.

name: Keyring trust domain
description: A keyring identifies a trust scope: thread-keyring (per-thread), process-keyring, session-keyring, user-keyring, user-session-keyring, persistent-user-keyring (cross-session), .dns_resolver / .request-key-auth (system). Permissions per-key control read/write/search/link/setattr/view bits separately for possessor/user/group/other.

name: Credential inheritance across exec/clone
description: How RUID/EUID/SUID/FSUID and capabilities propagate. fork/clone: copied verbatim. execve: reset per the cap-transition rules in capabilities(7) sections 'Capabilities and execution of programs by root' and 'Transformation of capabilities during execve()'. Setuid bit re-sets EUID/SUID to file owner unless caller has PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS (then setuid is no-op).

name: PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS bit
description: One-way per-thread bit (set via prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS, 1)) that causes execve(2) to NOT grant privileges via setuid bits or file capabilities. Inherited across fork/clone/execve. Required for unprivileged seccomp filter installation. The cornerstone of confined process startup; systemd's `NoNewPrivileges=yes` and Docker's default for non-root containers set it.

name: Process image replacement (execve semantics)
description: Calling execve(2) replaces the entire address space (text/data/heap/stack/mmaps) with the new program's, while preserving PID, parent, file descriptors not marked O_CLOEXEC, signal masks (but not handlers — those reset to defaults), and resource limits. The reason 'fork+exec' is the universal Unix process-creation idiom — the fork is for keeping the parent alive; the exec is the actual program switch.

name: Copy-on-write fork semantics
description: fork(2) doesn't physically duplicate the parent's address space — it shares the pages read-only and copies on write. RSS of the child immediately after fork is near-zero; only modified pages get duplicated. This is why fork+exec is cheap for shells (no real copy, then execve discards everything) but costly when the parent has a large heap that the child mutates.

name: vfork(2) parent-blocking semantics
description: Legacy fork variant where the child shares the parent's address space (not COW — actually shared) until the child calls execve or _exit. The parent is suspended. Modern Linux implements vfork() as clone(CLONE_VM|CLONE_VFORK|SIGCHLD). Faster than fork on systems without COW; obsolete on COW systems but still useful in narrow exec-immediately patterns.

name: DAC (discretionary access control) model
description: Classic Unix file permissions: owner/group/other × read/write/execute, plus setuid/setgid/sticky. Each process has UID + GIDs; each file has owner UID + group GID + 9 mode bits. Per-file ACLs (xattrs) extend this. Capabilities augment for fine-grained privileged operations. LSMs add MAC on top.

name: POSIX ACLs vs DAC mode bits
description: ACLs are stored in xattrs (system.posix_acl_access, system.posix_acl_default) and let you grant per-user/per-group permissions beyond the owner/group/other tuple. Mask entry caps the effective permissions of all named entries. Detail in linux/filesystem.

name: OOM killer
description: Kernel mechanism that selects and SIGKILLs a process when memory cannot be allocated and overcommit can't be honored. Score per process: oom_score (sum of factors) adjusted by oom_score_adj (-1000 to +1000; -1000 is OOM-immune). MemoryMax in cgroup v2 triggers a per-cgroup OOM kill. Containers see exit code 137 (128 + 9 = SIGKILL).

name: oom_score_adj
description: Per-process tunable bias (-1000 to +1000) added to the OOM score. -1000 = never kill. +1000 = kill first. Set via /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj or systemd's OOMScoreAdjust=. Container runtimes often set the container init's adj to -500 so the OOM killer prefers user processes.

name: Unified vs legacy cgroup controllers
description: v2 introduces a few new controllers (io supersedes blkio with better tracking), reuses some (cpu, memory, pids), and drops some (net_cls, net_prio went to BPF/eBPF; devices went to BPF-LSM). 'Hybrid' mode mounts v2 + v1 simultaneously but a controller can be active in only one. Migration is one-way per-controller.

name: Namespace FS membership via /proc/<pid>/ns/
description: Each namespace appears as a magic symlink in /proc/<pid>/ns/{pid,user,mnt,ipc,uts,net,cgroup,time}. The link target is a unique 'ns:[<inode>]' identifier; two processes in the same namespace have identical targets. setns(2) takes an open FD on these. nsenter -t PID -p -m -n is just open()s of these files plus setns().

name: Pressure Stall Information (PSI)
description: Per-cgroup metric exposing how much time tasks were blocked on CPU/memory/IO contention. /sys/fs/cgroup/<cg>/cpu.pressure, memory.pressure, io.pressure. Format: 'some avg10=… avg60=… avg300=… total=…' and 'full avg10=…'. The data behind systemd's MemoryPressureWatch and oomd's killing decisions.

name: Process lifecycle
description: created (forked, not yet scheduled) → running → sleeping (interruptible/uninterruptible) → stopped (SIGSTOP/SIGTSTP) → zombie (exited, parent hasn't wait()ed) → reaped. /proc/<pid>/status State field reports the kernel's view ('R', 'S', 'D', 'T', 'Z'). 'D' (uninterruptible) typically means a syscall is blocked in IO and cannot be killed even by SIGKILL — most common cause of unkillable processes.

name: Zombie reaping
description: Process that exited but whose exit-status hasn't been collected by its parent via wait(2)/waitpid/waitid stays as a zombie (/proc entry with State=Z, no other resources). PID-1 of a namespace is responsible for reaping orphans (children whose original parent exited and were reparented). Without a reaper, zombies accumulate until pid-max — the 'docker zombie problem' tini/dumb-init solves.

name: Subreaper (PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER)
description: Per-process attribute: when set, orphaned descendants reparent to this process instead of pid 1. Lets a service supervisor catch its own grandchildren without needing to actually be pid 1. systemd uses this for user@.service scope.

name: wait/waitpid/waitid family
description: Syscalls that retrieve a child's exit status: wait(2) — any child; waitpid(2) — specific PID or process group; waitid(2) — full siginfo + flexible WNOHANG/WNOWAIT options. Required to reap zombies. SIGCHLD is delivered to the parent on child exit/stop/continue (configurable via sigaction's SA_NOCLDSTOP / SA_NOCLDWAIT).

name: Signal default actions
description: Per-signal default behavior when no handler installed: Term (terminate), Core (terminate + dump core), Ign (ignore), Stop (suspend), Cont (resume). E.g. SIGTERM=Term, SIGKILL=Term (uncatchable), SIGSEGV=Core, SIGCHLD=Ign, SIGSTOP=Stop, SIGCONT=Cont. signal(7) tabulates all 64.

name: Realtime signals
description: SIGRTMIN..SIGRTMAX (typically 32 signals). UNLIKE standard signals, RT signals queue (multiple deliveries don't merge), are delivered in priority order (lowest number first), and carry a sigval payload via sigqueue(3). RLIMIT_SIGPENDING caps the per-user queue depth. Used by glibc internally (NPTL thread cancellation, timers); rarely by app code.

name: cgroup.procs vs cgroup.threads
description: cgroup.procs adds a process (and all its threads) to the cgroup. cgroup.threads adds a single thread (requires the cgroup's type to be 'threaded'). 'threaded' cgroups can only contain threads of a single process and only thread-aware controllers (cpu, perf_event, pids) work. The default 'domain' type is what containers use.

name: cgroup.events file
description: Per-cgroup file exposing 'populated' (any descendant has processes) and 'frozen' (cgroup.freeze=1 took effect) flags. Watchable via inotify or the file's poll interface — the canonical way to wait for 'cgroup is empty' (e.g., systemd's main-PID death detection).

name: cgroup freeze
description: Atomically suspends every process in a cgroup (and descendants). Write 1 to cgroup.freeze. Useful for snapshot consistency, debugging, CRIU-style checkpoint. Replaces the v1 freezer controller; works on every v2 cgroup without requiring a special controller.

name: Memory overcommit
description: vm.overcommit_memory sysctl: 0 (heuristic: refuse obviously-too-large allocs), 1 (always allow — never NULL from malloc), 2 (strict: total commit ≤ vm.overcommit_ratio% of RAM + swap). Heuristic mode (default) is why Java often gets MAP_FAILED only when actually touching pages; strict mode is recommended for memory-sensitive servers. malloc()=NULL ↔ touched-page=OOM-kill is the consequence chain.

name: Virtual memory areas (VMAs)
description: Per-process list of mapped regions: text, data, heap, stack, mmap'd files, shared libraries, anonymous mmaps. Visible in /proc/<pid>/maps (path + start-end + perms + offset + dev:inode). RLIMIT_AS caps total VMA size; vm.max_map_count limits the count (some apps need it raised — Elasticsearch is the famous case).

name: Thread group ID (TGID)
description: The PID of the first thread in a process; same value returned by getpid() in every thread of that process. The kernel's per-thread ID is what /proc/<pid>/task/<tid> uses; TGID = the user-visible 'process' identifier. This is why 'ps -L' shows multiple lines per process and 'top -H' splits threads.

name: Process state R (running)
description: On CPU or runnable on the run queue. /proc/<pid>/status State='R (running)'. Doesn't necessarily mean currently executing — could be waiting for a CPU.

name: Process state S (interruptible sleep)
description: Blocked in a syscall waiting for an event, but signal-deliverable. /proc/<pid>/status State='S (sleeping)'. Most idle daemons (sshd, init) live here.

name: Process state D (uninterruptible sleep)
description: Blocked in kernel, signals deferred. Cannot be killed (even SIGKILL doesn't interrupt). Usually a syscall stuck in IO (NFS hang, slow disk, broken USB). /proc/<pid>/status State='D (disk sleep)'. The 'reboot to recover' state.

name: Process state T (stopped)
description: Suspended via SIGSTOP/SIGTSTP/SIGTTIN/SIGTTOU or by ptrace tracer. Resumed by SIGCONT. /proc/<pid>/status State='T (stopped)' or 't (tracing stop)'.

name: Process state Z (zombie)
description: Exited; awaiting wait() by parent. Holds only the /proc/<pid>/ entry — no memory, no FDs. /proc/<pid>/status State='Z (zombie)'. Accumulates if pid-1 doesn't reap (the docker zombie problem).

name: Process state X (dead)
description: Process is being torn down by the kernel — transient state never visible to ps/top under normal conditions.

name: Process state t (tracing stop)
description: Stopped by ptrace tracer (e.g. strace, gdb attached). Distinct from 'T' (signal-induced stop) in /proc/<pid>/status.

name: Signal state: pending
description: Signal delivered but not yet handled because mask blocks it. SigPnd and ShdPnd lines in /proc/<pid>/status. Standard signals collapse multiple pending into one; RT signals queue.

name: Signal state: blocked
description: In the per-thread signal mask — pending instead of delivered. SigBlk in /proc/<pid>/status.

name: Signal state: ignored
description: Disposition is SIG_IGN — kernel discards on delivery. SigIgn in /proc/<pid>/status. Note: PID 1 ignores ALL signals it has no handler for, even if disposition is SIG_DFL — see pid-1-init-semantics.

name: Signal state: caught
description: User-installed handler will run on delivery. SigCgt in /proc/<pid>/status.

name: cgroup state: populated
description: At least one descendant cgroup contains a process. Visible as `populated 1` in cgroup.events. Useful signal for service supervisors to detect that all child processes have exited.

name: cgroup state: frozen
description: cgroup.freeze=1 has fully taken effect — every process in subtree is suspended. Visible as `frozen 1` in cgroup.events. Atomic relative to syscall entry (in-progress syscalls complete; new ones block until thaw).

name: cgroup subsystem
description: The kernel's process grouping + resource control framework. Code under kernel/cgroup/. Provides the cgroupfs interface mounted at /sys/fs/cgroup. Per-controller subsystems (memory, cpu, io, pids, hugetlb, rdma, misc, cpuset, cgroup-bpf) plug in via the cgroup_subsys interface.

name: namespace subsystem
description: Kernel infrastructure providing the 8 namespace types. Per-namespace data structures hang off task_struct->nsproxy. Lifetime is reference-counted; namespace dies when last process referencing it (including via /proc/<pid>/ns/* open FDs and bind-mounts) exits.

name: LSM subsystem
description: Kernel framework for stackable mandatory access control. Modules register hook implementations called at security-relevant points (file open, exec, mmap, capability check, etc.). Order in which LSMs run is configurable via lsm= boot parameter. Active LSMs visible in /sys/kernel/security/lsm.

name: keyrings subsystem
description: In-kernel key storage and management. Code under security/keys/. Used by dm-crypt (LUKS key passing), NFSv4 idmap, ecryptfs, fscrypt, and any service needing secrets the kernel itself uses without exposing them to userspace.

name: signals subsystem
description: Kernel infrastructure for asynchronous notification of processes. Per-thread sigqueue + per-process shared queue. Signal delivery happens at syscall return / interrupt return / scheduler entry. Code in kernel/signal.c.

name: NPTL pthreads implementation
description: glibc's POSIX threads layer (Native POSIX Thread Library). Maps each pthread to a kernel task (1:1 model, replacing the older M:N LinuxThreads). Uses futexes for fast user-space synchronization (mutex, cond, rwlock, barrier).

name: OOM killer subsystem
description: Kernel code (mm/oom_kill.c) that selects victims when memory is exhausted. Per-cgroup OOM killer in cgroup v2 + memory.max constraints; global OOM kicks in when entire host hits a wall. Score function blends RSS, oom_score_adj, and other factors; recursion through ancestor cgroups when MemoryHigh/Max are set.

name: seccomp subsystem
description: The secure-computing (syscall filtering) facility. Code in kernel/seccomp.c. Plugs into syscall entry to evaluate the filter chain before syscall execution. Audit integration logs SECCOMP_RET_LOG actions to auditd.

name: /proc/sys (sysctl tree)
description: Procfs subtree exposing kernel tunables — vm.*, kernel.*, fs.*, net.* (ownership of net.* belongs in linux/networking). Read/write via /proc/sys/<path> or via sysctl(8). Persistent settings in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf.

name: /proc/<pid>/ns/* namespace links
description: Magic symlinks identifying each namespace the process belongs to. setns(2) takes an open FD on these. Bind-mountable to keep a namespace alive after its last process exits.

name: /proc/<pid>/uid_map
description: User namespace UID translation table. Format: 'inside-uid host-uid count' lines. Write-once after process is in a userns. Companion: /proc/<pid>/gid_map (with /proc/<pid>/setgroups gating).

name: /proc/<pid>/cgroup
description: Per-process cgroup membership. Format: 'hierarchy-id:controller-list:cgroup-path'. v2 entries have hierarchy-id 0 and empty controller-list. Quick way to see which cgroup (and thus which container) a PID belongs to.

name: /proc/<pid>/status
description: Human-readable per-process state. Lines: Name, State, Tgid, Pid, PPid, Uid (real/eff/saved/fs), Gid, FDSize, VmPeak/VmSize/VmRSS/VmData/VmStk, Threads, NSpid (PIDs in each namespace), CapInh/CapPrm/CapEff/CapBnd/CapAmb (capability sets as hex), Seccomp (0/1/2), SigQ/SigPnd/ShdPnd/SigBlk/SigIgn/SigCgt (signal masks).

name: /sys/fs/cgroup (cgroupfs mount point)
description: Standard mount point for the cgroup pseudo-filesystem. v2: a single tree. v1: per-controller subdirs (cpu/, memory/, blkio/, …). systemd manages the layout: /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/<unit>/, user.slice/user-<uid>.slice/, …

name: /etc/security/limits.conf
description: PAM-honored ulimit defaults set at login. Per-user/group soft and hard limits for nofile, nproc, fsize, memlock, stack, etc. Effective only for sessions opened via PAM (login, sshd, su); systemd-managed services use the unit's LimitX= directives instead.

name: /proc/cmdline
description: Read-only view of the kernel command line booted with. Source for diagnosing 'is X enabled?' (e.g. cgroup_no_v1=, systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=, mitigations=, root=).

name: OOM killer policy
description: The kernel selects an OOM victim by scoring every task: oom_score = scaled RSS + oom_score_adj * (totalpages / 1000). Highest non-immune (oom_score_adj != -1000) wins. Per-cgroup OOM (memory.oom.group=1) kills every process in the cgroup atomically. Global OOM picks across the whole system.

name: Default keyring lookup order
description: When a key is requested without an explicit keyring: thread-keyring → process-keyring → session-keyring → user-session-keyring → user-keyring → user-default-session-keyring → group-keyring (if any). request_key(2) follows this chain and may invoke /sbin/request-key to instantiate a missing key from userspace.

name: memory.events file
description: Per-cgroup memory pressure event counters. Lines: low (memory.low breached), high (memory.high triggered throttling), max (memory.max hit, leading to OOM if reclaim fails), oom (cgroup OOM occurred), oom_kill (count of processes killed by cgroup OOM). Watching memory.events with inotify is how systemd-oomd / oomd act before global OOM kicks in.

name: cpu.stat file
description: Per-cgroup CPU accounting. Fields: usage_usec (total CPU time), user_usec, system_usec, nr_periods (CFS periods elapsed), nr_throttled (periods throttled), throttled_usec (time spent throttled). When user reports 'CPU is throttled even though usage is low', this is where the truth is.

name: io.stat file
description: Per-cgroup per-device IO accounting. Lines: '<major>:<minor> rbytes=N wbytes=N rios=N wios=N dbytes=N dios=N'. Doesn't include filesystem-cache hits — only IO that hit the block layer.

name: MS_SHARED mount propagation
description: Default for systemd-managed roots. New mounts propagate bidirectionally between peer mounts. Containers that bind-mount /var/lib/docker would see (and be seen by) the host's view if propagation isn't reset.

name: MS_PRIVATE mount propagation
description: No mount events propagate. The runc default for the container's root after pivot_root — container mounts are isolated from host.

name: MS_SLAVE mount propagation
description: Receives propagation from master peer group, doesn't propagate back. Useful for /sys/fs/cgroup inside containers — host cgroup remounts visible inside, container mounts stay inside.

name: MS_UNBINDABLE mount propagation
description: Cannot be the source of a bind-mount. Niche — used to prevent escape via mount manipulation in unusual setups.

name: PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS feature
description: The prctl operation that sets the no_new_privs bit. Permanent (cannot be cleared). Inherited across fork/exec. Required for unprivileged seccomp filter installation. Foundation of confined process startup.

name: PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER feature
description: prctl operation marking a process as the reaper for orphaned descendants. Lets a service manager catch SIGCHLD for grandchildren without becoming pid 1.

name: PR_SET_SECUREBITS feature
description: Capability-system tweaks: SECBIT_NOROOT (UID 0 doesn't get root caps), SECBIT_NO_SETUID_FIXUP (no cap manipulation on UID change), SECBIT_KEEP_CAPS (preserve P set across UID change to non-zero), and locked variants. Each has a *_LOCKED counterpart that prevents future changes.

name: setpriority(2)/nice(2)
description: Adjust per-process scheduling 'nice' value (-20 to +19; lower = higher priority). Non-CAP_SYS_NICE callers can only raise nice (lower priority). Affects CFS share allocation. systemd's `Nice=` directive.

name: ionice / IO scheduling priority
description: Per-process IO scheduling class: real-time (0), best-effort (1, default), idle (3). Tunable via ioprio_set(2) syscall or ionice(1). Applies under CFQ/BFQ schedulers; less impact under mq-deadline/none.

name: sched_setaffinity(2)
description: Pin a process/thread to a subset of CPUs. Inherited across fork. Container runtimes use this for `--cpuset-cpus`. Inverse: sched_getaffinity gets the current mask.

name: setsid(2)/setpgid(2)
description: Process group / session manipulation. setsid creates a new session (process becomes session leader, no controlling terminal). setpgid moves a process between groups for job control. Used by daemons to detach from terminal at startup.
